title: Experimental and numerical investigations on the mean stress effect on the fatigue of thin-walled tubular joints
abstract: Abstract Welded hollow section joints play a key role in lightweight automotive design, particularly in applications involving buses, trucks, and special-purpose vehicles. High-strength steels enable significant efficiency gains, especially when used in thin-walled constructions that fully exploit their load-bearing potential. In such applications, rectangular hollow section joints with a chord to brace ratio of 1 are widely used and exhibit favorable fatigue performance. However, accurately assessing the fatigue strength of these joints remains a challenge, particularly due to mean stress effects arising from service loads and welding-induced residual stresses. Current design codes address these effects inconsistently: the nominal stress approach often neglects them or provides conservative estimates, while the structural stress concept defined in ISO 14347 is not suitable for wall thicknesses below 4 mm. The effective notch stress approach, although more refined, assumes R-ratio-independent behavior for non-stress-relieved joints and does not differentiate between steel grades. To address these limitations, fatigue tests were conducted within the FOSTA P1603 research project at Munich University of Applied Sciences on X-joints under varying load ratios. The results were supplemented with numerical analyses to refine the assessment methods used in the nominal and the effective notch stress approach. This study contributes to a more accurate fatigue evaluation of thin-walled, high-strength steel joints and aims to extend the applicability of current design guidelines.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: In the field of commercial and special vehicle construction, structural components are subjected to intensive structural loading. At the same time, the overall weight must be minimized to ensure both structural integrity and increased payload capacity. Lightweight design therefore plays a key role in enhancing transport efficiency and overall vehicle performance.

In addition to functional requirements, increasing demands for energy efficiency and resource conservation are placing greater challenges on designers and engineers. As a result, welded hollow section joints have become increasingly established in recent years, offering an effective solution for combining structural reliability with weight reduction. A key challenge in these welded lightweight structures lies in their susceptibility to fatigue loading, which remains the predominant failure mechanism under cyclic stresses. Fatigue-induced damage typically initiates and propagates unnoticed, often resulting in sudden and unexpected failure. Consequently, a detailed understanding of fatigue behavior is essential to ensure the safe and durable design of welded joints, especially in thin-walled, high-strength steel applications commonly used in the vehicle industry.

One of the defining features of welded hollow section joints is the local increase in stiffness at the intersection of chord and brace. This geometric discontinuity causes high local stress concentration, which significantly influences the crack initiation phase and thus determines the overall fatigue behavior of the structure. The fatigue performance of such joints is therefore strongly dependent on several geometric relationships such as the chord to brace ratio or the wall thickness. Among the various configurations, joints with equal chord to brace ratio have demonstrated particularly favorable fatigue performance [ 1 ], primarily due to a more uniform load path during force transmission.

To address fatigue-related challenges while maintaining efficiency and payload capacity, the use of high- and ultra-high-strength steels is becoming increasingly common [ 2 ]. These modern materials can help reduce weight by making use of their specific mechanical properties. High ductility austenitic steels in particular have gained importance in the vehicle industry in recent years [ 3 ], also in non-crash relevant parts. However, the effectiveness of this lightweight strategy remains a subject of discussion. Studies such as Gurney [ 4 ] have shown that increasing the yield strength of the base material offers only limited benefits in highly notched structures. The main advantage is seen in the relatively short crack initiation phase, whereas the crack propagation phase appears to be largely independent of the material strength [ 5 ].

Due to high local stress concentration at the weld toe, plastic deformation occurs regardless of the base material, leading to partial relaxation of residual stresses. According to [ 12 ,  13 ] the effective mean stress is a superposition of the applied mean stress and the relaxed residual stress and thus differs from the nominal value.

Accordingly, modern design recommendations do not apply direct correction for applied load mean stress but instead account for residual stresses. For instance, the IIW guideline [ 14 ] introduces an enhancement factor  f ( R ) which considers residual stress levels and modifies the derived FAT class accordingly (Fig.  1 ). Fig. 1 Enhancement factor f(R) based on [ 14 ]

This limitation stems from the prevailing assumption that welded joints are affected by high tensile residual stresses. As demonstrated in [ 16 ], fatigue cracks tend to initiate at typical critical locations and propagate into zones of high tensile residual stress. Nevertheless, fatigue tests under fully compressive loads have demonstrated longer lifetimes compared to tensile loads [ 17 ,  18 ] attributable to the crack-flank closure effects under compressive mean stress, which reduce crack growth rates.

In the present field of application, however, the structural components are significantly smaller in scale compared to those investigated by Fisher et al. [ 11 ]. As a result, welding-induced residual stresses are assumed to be moderate to low. This suggests that the applied load mean stress may indeed influence fatigue life, even in fully tensile regimes, meaning that fatigue strength is no longer solely a function of stress range. Due to the relatively short crack initiation phase in welded hollow section joints, residual stresses tend to relax during crack propagation. As a result, the influence of load mean stress increases significantly in this phase.

In addition, a previous project [ 19 ] investigating sequence effects on the life estimation of welded tubes revealed significant deviations in the treatment of mean stress influence compared to common design guidelines [ 20 ,  21 ]. To investigate this effect, the present study examines the fatigue performance of rectangular joints without post-weld treatment for different load mean stresses, based on tests performed within the project FOSTA P1603 [ 22 ]. Axial and bending loading is applied via the brace member, and up to four different load ratios are used to assess the influence of load mean stress on the fatigue behavior of welded hollow section joints.

sections.heading: Materials
paragraphs: The materials used in this study were selected in consultation with the project partner of [ 22 ] to evaluate their potential application in welded bus and commercial vehicle structures. Due to the increasing demand for lightweight construction and the more stringent carbon dioxide regulations, there is a growing need to replace conventional structural steel grades with higher-strength alternatives to reduce vehicle weight and increase payload capacity.

The first material investigated was S460MH, a fine-grain structural steel classified under DIN 10219-1 [ 23 ] (material number 1.8849). This thermomechanically rolled, high-strength, low-alloy steel is commonly used in the bus and commercial vehicle industry due to its good weldability and a balanced combination of strength and toughness that meets typical industry requirements.

The main chemical composition of the materials investigated can be seen in mass percent in Table  3 . The composition of the fine-grain structural steel is specified according to DIN EN 10219-1 [ 23 ], while the chemical composition of the austenitic steel 1.4678 is based on supplier-provided data from the respective melting process.

sections.heading: Specimens
Fatigue tests
Fatigue assessment nominal stress approach
paragraphs: These findings suggest a significantly stronger mean stress sensitivity in the austenitic steel specimens, compared to the fine-grain structural steel specimens, along with generally higher fatigue strength. Across all bending tests and all corresponding load ratios, the austenitic steel 1.4678 consistently demonstrates superior fatigue performance under identical boundary conditions and failure modes. It should be reiterated that although the test specimens are subject to residual welding stresses, they are not subject to assembly stresses due to the bending load test setups.

It is evident that the austenitic steel specimens subjected to axial compression exhibit an unexpected failure pattern. Despite the application of a constant compressive load, failures occur in a relatively uniform manner and appear to be governed by a failure mechanism that has not yet been fully understood or accounted for. In contrast to the behavior observed in tensile tests, this results in a lower fatigue strength compared to the corresponding specimens made of 1.8849.

Fatigue assessment of effective notch stress approach (ENS)
paragraphs: In principle, the recommended FAT class according to the IIW recommendation applies independently of the material for the general category of steel. However, the significantly different fatigue strengths of the investigated austenitic steel compared to the fine-grained structural steel, as well as the influence of the loading type, require a separate evaluation of the effective notch stress. As a result, separate SN curves are derived for the fine-grain structural steel 1.8849 and the austenitic steel 1.4678, and for the different load types.

sections.heading: Mean stress evaluation of the effective notch stress results
paragraphs: Due to the differing characteristics of the individual test results, a joint evaluation, as originally intended in the effective notch stress concept, does not appear appropriate. Therefore, all materials and loading conditions were analyzed separately. Since the linear-elastic notch stress factors are identical for the respective loading cases, the differences in fatigue strength between the loading types remain, but the individual values are merely shifted upward by a constant factor. Consequently, the slopes and thus the resulting mean stress sensitivities remain unchanged. The corresponding values are identical to those obtained from the nominal stress approach and can be found in Table  7 .

sections.heading: Residual stress measurement
paragraphs: The influence of welding residual stresses, whether caused by shrinkage or phase transformation, on the fatigue behavior of structures has already been investigated [ 34 ,  35 ]. These studies include partwise not only structural steels but also fine-grain steels. The effect of residual stresses in austenitic steels has likewise been the subject of prior research [ 36 ].

Current design recommendations generally assume that residual stresses are in the range of the base material’s yield strength, unless more precise data (e.g., from measurements) are available to the designer. Since such measurements are often costly or not non-destructive, this assumption is commonly relied upon. As a result, the widely accepted view has emerged that residual stresses at yield level are always present, rendering the applied load mean stress irrelevant and making fatigue life a function solely of the stress range.

To evaluate the influence of welding residual stresses on mean stress effects in the present study, residual stress measurements were conducted on specimens made of both fine-grain structural steel and austenitic steel. The measurements were performed by the University of Kassel, Germany, using X-ray diffraction on unloaded specimens. Additionally, residual stress data from a previous project [ 19 ] are included. These data were obtained from specimens that were also used in the fatigue tests presented in this study.

Figure  15  shows the longitudinal residual stress distributions for both materials, including the standard deviations of the measurements. The longitudinal direction refers to the direction along the brace axis. Consequently, the measured stresses represent the stress component transverse to the weld line at the brace–chord intersection. Fig. 15 Longitudinal residual stresses for fine-grain structural steel 1.8849 in red and austenitic steel 1.4678 in blue

As expected, the residual stress distribution in the specimens made of fine-grained structural steel shows no significant tensile residual stresses. Instead, a consistent compressive stress profile is observed, with values steadily decreasing toward the weld seam center. No notable differences were identified between measurement section MS0, located at the center of the brace tube, and MS4, positioned near the tube corner. In both sections, a slight increase in longitudinal compressive residual stresses is observed immediately after the weld centerline, but the values remain entirely within the compressive range.

The increased longitudinal residual stresses observed in the corner areas result from a superposition of welding-induced stresses and manufacturing-induced residual stresses due to the forming process at the corner radius.

Additionally, it can be observed that the residual stress profiles obtained from measurement sections MS0 and MS4 in this study are in good agreement with the data from the previous project, showing no relevant deviations in trend or magnitude.

The scatter observed in the residual stress results is primarily attributed to local variations within the heat-affected zone (HAZ), which are assumed to arise from inconsistencies in the welding process. In particular, the weld start and end points, and thus the welding sequence, appear to have a significant influence on the resulting residual stress distribution.

Nevertheless, it becomes evident that the initially measured residual stresses alone are of limited relevance when assessing fatigue strength. Instead, the relaxed residual stresses, which are not accessible through the applied measurement methods, are of greater importance for understanding the actual fatigue behavior and the effect of mean stress. Moreover, the commonly held assumption that fatigue strength is independent of mean stress presumes that residual stresses at the critical weld toe reach yield strength levels. However, the present measurements clearly indicate that this condition is not generally met.

sections.heading: Discussion
paragraphs: The most significant mean stress influence was observed in the austenitic specimens under bending, which exhibited notably higher values of the mean stress sensitivity. This indicates a pronounced mean stress sensitivity of the high-toughness steel used. In addition, these bending specimens generally achieved considerably longer fatigue lives. In contrast, the axially loaded austenitic specimens showed significantly shorter fatigue lives than their bending counterparts, highlighting the need for further analysis. The fine-grain structural steel behaved largely as expected, with a moderate mean stress dependence. The relatively small reduction in fatigue observed in the axially loaded specimens may be attributed to the presence of assembly induced residual stresses.

As the results indicate, a combined evaluation of both steels with respect to the recommended FAT class of the ENS approach is not appropriate. The significantly higher fatigue life of the bending specimens made of high-strength steel is offset by the comparatively low performance of the axially loaded specimens, leading to an underestimation of the high-strength material. Conversely, the structural steel specimens exhibit lower fatigue strengths under tensile loading and higher strengths under fully compressive loading than suggested by the joint evaluation. Whereas the fine-grain structural steel shows the expected behavior reported in the literature, often not reaching the failure criterion due to compressive stresses, the austenitic steel specimens display a consistent failure pattern.

To capture the effect of residual welding stresses, additional residual stress measurements were performed. These measurements revealed significant differences in residual stress distribution between the fine-grain structural and austenitic steel. Notably, residual compressive stresses were consistently detected in the critical areas near the weld toe and the failure-relevant regions. To adequately describe the mechanisms and phenomena observed in the experiments to date, further investigations are currently being conducted. These include metallographic methods such as microsection imaging and hardness testing, as well as the evaluation of assembly induced stresses through strain gauge measurements, in order to clarify remaining uncertainties.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: The results clearly demonstrate a pronounced mean stress sensitivity in both materials, with lower mean stress consistently leading to longer fatigue lives. The most substantial sensitivity was observed in the austenitic steel under bending, which exhibited significantly higher fatigue strengths than all axial configurations and fine-grain structural steel. In contrast, the same material showed unexpectedly short fatigue lives under axial loading and a continuous failure pattern even under fully compressive conditions. These findings underline that fatigue behavior is strongly material-dependent despite the high notch sensitivity.

The ENS-based assessment further showed that a combined evaluation of both materials against a common FAT class is not appropriate, as it underestimates the benefits of the high-strength steel and overestimates the performance of the structural steel under tensile loading. While the high mean stress sensitivity and improved fatigue performance observed in this study highlight the potential of ultra-high-strength and high-toughness steels, these findings strictly apply to the investigated material 1.4678. Demonstrating whether similar behavior can be expected in other high-toughness or ultra-high-strength steels will require further experimental evidence.

Residual stress measurements confirm substantial differences between the two materials, with compressive residual stresses present near the weld toe in both cases. Overall, the results highlight that material-specific behavior, mean stress sensitivity, and residual stress effects must be explicitly considered to achieve reliable fatigue assessments of hollow section joints. Ongoing metallographic and experimental investigations will further clarify the underlying mechanisms.
